title: Ἄνθρωπος καὶ σάτυρος
part: The Man and the Satyr (Chambry 60 · Perry 35)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 60 (= Perry 35). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἄνθρωπόν ποτε λέγεται πρὸς σάτυρον φιλίαν σπείσασθαι.
sentences.tr: Anthrōpon pote legetai pros satyron philian speisasthai.
sentences.l: A man is said once to have made a friendship with a satyr.
sentences.i: It is said that a man once made a pact of friendship with a satyr.
sentences.n: σπένδομαι is properly to pour a libation, and so to make a solemn compact — the agreement is sworn over wine poured out. A satyr is a wild half-animal creature of the countryside in Dionysus' train, snub-nosed and horse-tailed in Greek art (the goat-legged figure is a later conflation), living outside human houses and human manners, which is what the ending turns on. λέγεται is impersonal with the accusative and infinitive, 'it is said that…'.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ χειμῶνος καταλαβόντος καὶ ψύχους γενομένου, ὁ ἄνθρωπος προσφέρων τὰς χεῖρας τῷ στόματι ἐπέπνει.
sentences.tr: Kai dē cheimōnos katalabontos kai psychous genomenou, ho anthrōpos prospherōn tas cheiras tōi stomati epepnei.
sentences.l: And indeed, winter having overtaken them and cold having come on, the man, bringing his hands to his mouth, breathed upon them.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes side by side set the scene before the main verb, χειμῶνος καταλαβόντος and ψύχους γενομένου — the regular way of laying out circumstances in these fables.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ σατύρου τὴν αἰτίαν ἐρομένου δι’ ἣν τοῦτο πράττει, ἔλεγεν ὅτι θερμαίνει τὰς χεῖρας διὰ τὸ κρύος.
sentences.tr: Tou de satyrou tēn aitian eromenou di' hēn touto prattei, elegen hoti thermainei tas cheiras dia to kryos.
sentences.l: And the satyr having asked the reason for which he was doing this, he said that he was warming his hands because of the frost.
sentences.i: When the satyr asked the reason why he did this, he said that he was warming his hands against the cold.
sentences.n: ὅτι θερμαίνει keeps the present tense of the speaker's own words after a past main verb; Greek reports speech with the tense actually used, where English shifts it back to 'he was warming'.

sentences.t: Ὕστερον δὲ παρατεθείσης αὐτοῖς τραπέζης καὶ προσφαγήματος θερμοῦ σφόδρα ὄντος, ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἀναιρούμενος κατὰ μικρὸν τῷ στόματι προσέφερε καὶ ἐφύσα.
sentences.tr: Hysteron de paratetheisēs autois trapezēs kai prosphagēmatos thermou sphodra ontos, ho anthrōpos anairoumenos kata mikron tōi stomati prosephere kai ephysa.
sentences.l: And later, a table having been set before them and the dish being very hot, the man, taking it up little by little, brought it to his mouth and blew.
sentences.n: τράπεζα is the small low table carried in with the food, so 'a table was set before them' simply means the meal was served. κατὰ μικρόν, 'bit by bit'.

sentences.t: Πυνθανομένου δὲ πάλιν τοῦ σατύρου τί τοῦτο ποιεῖ, ἔφασκε καταψύχειν τὸ ἔδεσμα, ἐπεὶ λίαν θερμόν ἐστι.
sentences.tr: Pynthanomenou de palin tou satyrou ti touto poiei, ephaske katapsychein to edesma, epei lian thermon esti.
sentences.l: And the satyr asking again what he was doing this for, he kept saying that he was cooling the food, since it was too hot.
sentences.i: When the satyr asked again why he was doing this, he said that he was cooling the food, since it was far too hot.
sentences.n: ἔφασκε takes a plain infinitive, καταψύχειν, where the sentence before used ὅτι with a finite verb: the two constructions stand side by side with no difference of sense.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος ἔφη πρὸς αὐτόν· « Ἀλλ’ ἀποτάσσομαί σου τῇ φιλίᾳ, ὦ οὗτος, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ στόματος καὶ τὸ θερμὸν καὶ τὸ ψυχρὸν ἐξιεῖς. »
sentences.tr: Kakeinos ephē pros auton· « All' apotassomai sou tēi philiāi, ō houtos, hoti ek tou autou stomatos kai to thermon kai to psychron exieis. »
sentences.l: And he said to him: « But I renounce your friendship, you there, because out of the same mouth you send out both the hot and the cold. »
sentences.n: ὦ οὗτος is a blunt way of hailing a man, near 'you there'. ἀποτάσσομαι with the dative is to take one's leave of, to be done with. The English proverb of blowing hot and cold comes from this fable.

sentences.t: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς περιφεύγειν δεῖ τὴν φιλίαν ὧν ἀμφίβολός ἐστιν ἡ διάθεσις.
sentences.tr: Atar oun kai hēmas peripheugein dei tēn philian hōn amphibolos estin hē diathesis.
sentences.l: So then we too must shun the friendship of those whose disposition is ambiguous.
sentences.n: This closing formula is not 'the story shows that…' but Ἀτὰρ οὖν καί, 'so then we too…', in which the fable turns and takes the reader in; it closes fables 23 and 245 the same way. ὧν is a genitive relative hanging on τὴν φιλίαν, 'the friendship of those whose…'. ἀμφίβολος is literally 'thrown at from both sides', of what can be taken two ways.
